In a patient with suspected acute interstitial nephritis, withdrawal of offending medications is the first step in management. C
Eosinophiluria and gallium 67 scanning have limited sensitivity and specificity. C

background.definition: Acute interstitial nephritis is characterized by an inflammatory infiltrate of the renal interstitium that results in acute renal failure.

list.listitem: Acute interstitial nephritis accounts for 15% of hospitalized cases of acute renal failure.
Acute interstitial nephritis is seen in 1% of biopsies performed for hematuria and proteinuria.

Medications are a common cause of acute interstitial nephritis, including NSAIDs, antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, rifampin, ciprofloxacin, sulfonamides, vancomycin, macrolides), proton pump inhibitors, diuretics (furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, triamterene) and anticonvulsants (phenytoin, valproate).
Infection (streptococci, Legionella, leptospirosis, Cytomegalovirus, HIV).
Autoimmune (sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren's syndrome, Wegener's granulomatosis).
Idiopathic.
Most evidence points to acute interstitial nephritis being the result of an immune-mediated pathologic process.
Antigen-driven activation of T cells causes a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction that results in an inflammatory infiltrate in the renal interstitium and damage to the renal tubules.
Histologic examination of the renal interstitium shows a mixture of predominantly T lymphocytes, monocytes, and macrophages. Plasma cells, eosinophils, and neutrophils may also be seen.
Extrarenal findings of hypersensitivity are less commonly seen than in earlier descriptions of acute interstitial nephritis. B
Testing for urinary eosinophils has limited clinical use. C
Studies of gallium 67 scanning have had variable results. C
Renal biopsy is necessary when there is diagnostic uncertainty. C
Most patients present with nonspecific signs and symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, and malaise.

One analysis found the classic findings of rash, fever, eosinophilia, and the complete triad in only 15%, 27%, 23%, and 10% of patients, respectively. Another study found oliguria, arthralgia, and loin pain in 51%, 45%, and 21% of patients.
The onset of renal insufficiency after exposure to an offending drug is variable, from 2 to 3 days for a drug to which the patient has been previously sensitized, and from months to years for NSAIDs.
NSAID-associated acute interstitial nephritis has several unique features: presence of nephrotic syndrome, delayed onset of renal dysfunction, and the absence of extrarenal features.
Urinalysis may show hematuria, proteinuria (<1 g/day, except in NSAID-induced acute interstitial nephritis), sterile pyuria, and eosinophiluria.
Urinary eosinophils are of limited clinical use. One study showed only a 40% sensitivity and 72% specificity.

Studies of gallium 67 scanning in diagnosing acute interstitial nephritis have had variable results. A study of 44 patients with biopsy-proven renal disease showed all 11 patients with acute interstitial nephritis had intensely positive gallium 67 scan results. Five of the 33 patients with nonacute interstitial nephritis renal disease also had intensely positive gallium 67 scan results. Other studies have shown lower sensitivities and specificities.
Renal biopsy is needed when the diagnosis is clinically uncertain.
See for an approach to the patient with suspected acute interstitial nephritis.
Withdrawal of potential offending medications is the most important treatment. C
Confirmation of acute interstitial nephritis by renal biopsy is recommended prior to initiation of immunosuppressive therapy. C
Corticosteroids may be considered if there is no improvement of the clinical status within 7 days of removing an offending medication. C
The prompt removal of the offending drug is most important. Supportive measures, including dialysis, may be necessary.
If there is no improvement in clinical status 4 to 7 days after removing the offending drug, consider a renal biopsy for confirmation of acute interstitial nephritis.

No RCTs of treatment of acute interstitial nephritis exist; treatment is based on retrospective studies. There is insufficient evidence for the efficacy and safety of corticosteroids for the treatment of drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis.
In patients with persistent renal insufficiency, consider starting prednisone at a dosage of 1 mg/kg/day for 1 to 2 weeks with a gradual taper over the next 4 to 8 weeks.
Cyclophosphamide and mycophenolate mofetil have also been used in patients who are steroid resistant or have contraindications to steroids.
In an analysis of 128 patients with acute interstitial nephritis, 65% of patients recovered renal function, 23% had partial renal impairment, and 12% required chronic dialysis. B

Patients with infection-induced and idiopathic acute interstitial nephritis typically recover renal function; approximately one-third of patients with drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, however, will have persistent renal insufficiency. B

Predictors of renal recovery include the duration of acute renal failure and the level of renal function several weeks after the diagnosis. Amount of interstitial infiltration, presence of granuloma, and tubular atrophy are associated with a higher risk of having persistent renal insufficiency. B

cell.label: Patient with acute renal failure and suspected acute interstitial nephritis
Stop all potential offending medications, monitor renal function and clinical status over 4-7 days
Continue supportive care, and document hypersensitivity reaction
Consider gallium scan and/or empiric treatment
Continue at same dose for 1-2 weeks, then taper over 4-8 weeks
